title: Sonali Bendre Chose Raakh Because It Scared Her. You Should Watch It for the Same Reason.
excerpt: The Paatal Lok creator's new series drops on Prime Video June 12. Ali Fazal plays a cop who can't stop thinking. Sonali Bendre plays a mother who can't stop searching.
body:
The trailer opens with a question that hits like a punch to the sternum: "Bacche kab se gayab hain?" How long have the children been missing?

https://youtube.com/watch?v=RdB_TgwLPqs

Set in late 1970s Delhi, at a time when parents let their kids play outside after dark without a second thought, Raakh begins with the disappearance of two teenagers — and unfolds into something far darker, far more psychologically claustrophobic, and far more unsettling than your average crime procedural. The series premieres on Amazon Prime Video on June 12, available in Hindi across India and in over 240 countries and territories worldwide.

Let's start with the pedigree, because it's staggering. Raakh is directed and executive produced by Prosit Roy, the filmmaker behind Pari and — more relevantly — the first season of Paatal Lok, one of the most acclaimed Indian series ever made. Created, written, and co-directed by Anusha Nandakumar and Sandeep Saket, the series is produced by Endemol Shine India in association with BhaDiPa. When these names come together, you don't get a show. You get a reckoning.

But the real headline is the casting.

Ali Fazal plays Sub-Inspector Jayprakash, a character he describes as "the unlikely cop" — an introvert thrust into the centre of a case that threatens to break him. Fazal, who's built a filmography that ranges from Mirzapur to Victoria & Abdul to Death on the Nile, brings what his co-creators call "a quiet ferocity" to the role. Jayprakash isn't the swaggering, whiskey-sipping detective archetype. He's flawed, conflicted, and constantly trying to prove himself within a political and social landscape that doesn't care whether he succeeds or fails.

"What makes Raakh truly compelling is that it is a character study as much as it is a police procedural." — Ali Fazal
https://www.instagram.com/p/DY6ni0GOg-I/

And then there's Sonali Bendre.

Bendre plays Mona Arora, the mother of the missing children, and her presence in this series carries a weight that extends beyond the script. After her very public battle with metastatic cancer in 2018 — a fight she documented with remarkable grace and honesty — Bendre has been selective to the point of near-invisibility in choosing projects. Her return here is deliberate, considered, and deeply personal.

"Raakh came to me at a time when I've become very conscious of the stories I choose to be part of. What drew me to it was how layered and emotionally complex it is. While it unfolds as a thriller, at its heart it is a deeply human story." — Sonali Bendre

She describes Mona as a woman who carries "both vulnerability and quiet strength," and if the trailer is any indication, Bendre has found a role worthy of the years she spent away. There's a stillness to her screen presence now that feels earned — the calm of someone who has already stared down something far more terrifying than a fictional villain.

Completing the lead trio is Aamir Bashir as Lt. Col. Ashok Arora, a military man defined by discipline and regimen who finds himself navigating grief that has no protocol, no chain of command, no solution. Bashir, one of Indian cinema's most consistently excellent actors (if you haven't seen Nair or his work in Delhi Crime, correct that immediately), called this "one of the most challenging experiences of my career."

The supporting cast is stacked: Rakesh Bedi, Dibyendu Bhattacharya (who was extraordinary in Paatal Lok), Akash Makhija, and Anshul Chauhan round out an ensemble built for sustained psychological tension rather than star-driven spectacle.

What makes Raakh particularly interesting for the diaspora is its setting. 1970s Delhi — with its Emergency-era paranoia, its crumbling civility, its sense that the social contract was quietly dissolving — is a period rarely explored on screen. For NRIs, especially those whose parents grew up in that India, the show promises something uncomfortably intimate: the recognition that the country they mythologize had its own darkness, hiding in plain sight.

Prosit Roy has said he initially resisted the project because he didn't want to do another crime show after Paatal Lok. What changed his mind was the realisation that Raakh "is not just another crime series. There is something more to it." He describes it as a story about identity, grief, ideology, and the psychology of evil — a series where even the investigating officer's inner life becomes part of the mystery.

Raakh premieres June 12 on Prime Video. Clear your evening.
